extracted.intended_audience: general literate readers and aspiring prose writers (readers of The Spectator)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and normative rules for composing humour and tasteful prose in essays and letters: how to produce effective wit, what linguistic affectations to avoid, and delivery practices that heighten comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: True humour: thought and representation
rubrics_metrics.description: "True Humour lies in the Thought, and arises from the Representation of Images in odd Circumstances, and uncommon Lights."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour should come from a felicitous thought and striking representation (odd circumstances/uncommon lights). The pleasant idea itself is the source of mirth; contrived or merely verbal tricks do not suffice. (Context: contrasts genuine humour with mere affected phraseology.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceal ridicule in gravity / serious delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: "A Jest is never uttered with a better Grace, than when it is accompanied with a serious Countenance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver jokes with a composed or serious manner to preserve surprise and increase effect. Revealing the joke too early (with a playful face or anticipatory phrasing) diminishes its force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pert phraseology (cant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit and Humour are ... poorly recommended by a Levity of Phrase, and that kind of Language which may be distinguished by the Name of Cant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Light, pert, or fashionable catch-phrases (the 'cant' of pretenders to humour) often supply vivacity but not true wit; they tend to pall rather than heighten mirth. Example: burlesque/low 'country wit' letters that rely on slangy turns of phrase rather than thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid pedantic/pompous learned diction
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two Extreams ... the other in the Affectation of strained and pompous Expressions, fetched from the learned Languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affecting learned Latinisms and strained pompous expressions produces pedantick humour: obscure, riddling lines that force readers to re‑read rather than enjoy. The essay provides a parody letter and a mock‑poem demonstrating how such overlearned style becomes alienating and comical for the wrong reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer genuine feeling to formal rhetorical rules in eloquence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Persons I am speaking of are our common Beggars ... I have seen more Eloquence in a Look from one of these despicable Creatures, than in the Eye of the fairest She.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: True eloquence springs from real feeling and circumstance rather than from slavish adherence to classical rules. Emotional authenticity (a look, gesture, or honest appeal) can be more persuasive than practiced rhetorical artifice; be mindful of manipulative displays of 'eloquence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Widowhood virtues (criteria of a worthy widow)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two Things in which consists chiefly the Glory of a Widow; The Love of her deceased Husband, and the Care of her Children: To which may be added ... Such a prudent Conduct as may do Honour to both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A virtuous widow is judged chiefly by faithful love to her dead husband and responsible care for her children; prudent conduct that honors both is a third quality. Historical examples (Andromache, Artemisia) and local customs (free-bench conditions) are given as exemplars and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for ancestry should be earned, not claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: This is an Honour to be receiv'd, not demanded, by the Descendants of great Men; and they who are apt to remind us of their Ancestors, only put us upon making Comparisons to their own Disadvantage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boasting of illustrious ancestry is criticized: merit does not transfer automatically to descendants. Genealogies often reveal mixed, humble origins; public displays of pedigree that demand deference are ridiculed (example: the family tree pruned to conceal lowly ancestors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fear: proper object and remedies (moral criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fear is a very powerful Passion ... there is nothing which deserves his Fear, but that beneficent Being who is his Friend, his Protector, his Father.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fear grounded in conscience/guilt is a warning; unjustified fear is vain and ought to be corrected. Practical remedies: fix thought on a higher protector (faith/religion), reflect that feared events may not occur, that if they do they may be more bearable than imagined, or that life may not reach the feared moment; cultivate resignation and reasoned courage (illustrated by Horace and the Book of Wisdom).
